Couple of thoughts: First, the 2% DNA is an average. Many of European descent have 4% or a bit more. And Neandertals also bred with Denisovans, who ranged from western Siberia over into East and Southeast Asia. So "what happened to them" could be simply, like Denisovans, they became some of us. But because they were far less in number, Neandertals were genetically swamped by waves of sapiens coming up from Africa. 

Second, the writer doesn't bring up language. Many anthropologists think modern Homo sapiens had brains particularly enhanced for complex social speech, which in turn supported coordinated group hunting of late Pleistocene herd animals. Think reindeer and horse. Neandertals might not have needed it; they hunted and gathered differently. 

Mainly glad we're jettisoning this tired pejorative about slouching, apelike Neandertals. Wasn't even supported by data when the French fabricated it over a century ago.

There is no reason that general-release AI chatbots need to know how to hack a computer server, how to create a highly contagious pathogen, or how to make explosives. If they don’t know how, they can’t tell anyone. Regulations should require tech companies to curate their training data to exclude these dangerous topics. Special-purpose AIs could be trained on any one regulated subject – a hacker AI for use only by software companies to find vulnerabilities in their software, for example. Or a bio-expert AI for use only by medical research companies. Access to these AIs will be highly regulated, require a license, and tightly monitored, just as we regulate the handling of radioactive materials. The rest of us will have bots that simply won’t know how to do these things. This is not a complete solution, but it is a definable goal with a testable result. Regulations to accomplish this can be written and enforced. We’ve been trying to perfect alignment for years; it’s time to try something else.

I am saddened to think that Walter Koenig did not contribute much to Star Trek.  In a literal sense, perhaps he's right in that, in many episodes, he had few lines.

But, there's more to the cinematic arts than just lines of dialog or acting overall.  Sometimes, a character is an important part of the visual scenery.  For instance, when one watches Woody Allen's "Manhattan", Manhattan is an important part of the film.  It does no acting or say any dialog, but its presence in the film is unmistakeable and an important part of the "feel" of the film.  It wouldn't be the same movie even if it was filmed elsewhere.  The ending, with images of Manhattan while "Rhapsody in Blue" is playing contributes to the emotional impact.

And, like Manhattan is to "Manhattan", the Enterprise is to "Star Trek".  But, so were characters like Uhura, Sulu, and Chekov as part of the bridge crew or Nurse Chapel in sick bay.  
They, too, were an important part of Star Trek.  Even if the lines are perfunctory, the viewer seeing them has a sense of normalcy.  For instance, to not see Chekov on the bridge would immediately invite questions to the astute viewer.  Chekov on the bridge, even with minimal or no lines, brings comfort like a favorite pair of shoes or sweatshirt or song....

Had Walter Koenig not made Chekov enjoyable, the character would have been removed.  This illustrates that acting is more than dialog and performance and that being part of the scenery is often just as important.

Many posting here have wondered about how while private property is usually individual responsibility, states often step-in for private bridges wiped out by massive disasters like Hurricane Helene. 

It often comes down to several factors. Many mountain homes and whole neighborhoods are left completely stranded without a private bridge. State and federal agencies step in so emergency services (fire, EMS, police) can access residents and deliver basic utilities.

Rebuilding a bridge costs anywhere from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of dollars; a cost most single households or small HOAs cannot afford. Without public bridge assistance or temporary structures, properties become permanently uninhabitable, destroying tax bases and worsening housing crises.

Private bridges often link directly to public roads. Leaving them collapsed creates safety hazards, blocks waterways (increasing future flood risks), and disrupts local economic recovery.

Because public funds legally face restrictions against spending on private property, states typically use special disaster relief programs or federal funding (like FEMA public assistance exceptions) to build temporary or permanent access, balancing public safety needs against standard legal boundaries.

I’ve watched interviews with the various heads of the big AI companies where they describe a utopia where we don’t have to work and we can pursue some higher purpose. What never is addressed is, does that include the millions who today live in poverty around the world? Currently they have inadequate housing, food, medical care, etc. are they suddenly going to be meandering lush parks contemplating philosophy? comments.body: I think AI can be helpful as long as human operators direct the interaction, set boundaries, require primary references and maintain a critical filter on all sources and outputs. The human never shares, let alone surrenders, the role of executive director. When the AI, following its commercialized programming, starts asking a lot of questions, changing the subject or encouraging future meetings with its distinctive saccharine murmur, the answer is always: We’re done here. All this takes skill and discipline but nothing that couldn’t be taught in middle school. The other day while watching a Kubrick film I started to think of examples of Kubrick’s dark, extremely dry physical humor at the expense of authority, including the staff meeting scene on the space station in 2001. I decided to ask an AI for any examples it could come up with, plus examples of media employing that style of humor today. The exchange lasted a few minutes and I learned something. Now, if only Kubrick were here with us to do a Strangelove take on AI corporate culture.

When the sun is high above these glass-clad 1000-foot buildings, the reflected light is going to shine on something, and somebody, in the city. I hope the designers take that into account when plotting their designs.

I can’t meet clients with my belly exposed, and at 5'2", oversized clothing overwhelms my frame. Now in my second pregnancy, I’ve developed a formula that allows me to maintain my personal style without resorting to expensive, often dowdy maternity clothing. Like Ms. Friedman, I rely on stretch knits as well as bias-cut silk dresses sized up and dresses with smocking. Nearly every maternity-specific purchase I’ve made, apart from exercise leggings, has been a regret. Most are useful only briefly and don't transition well postpartum. My solution has been to buy a small, carefully edited wardrobe secondhand through Poshmark and The RealReal, sizing up one or two sizes. My first pregnancy had a summer third trimester, when I lived in sleeveless knits and smocked dresses from brands like Doen. This time, with a winter third trimester, I've gravitated toward bias-cut silk dresses layered with jackets, long-sleeved knit dresses, and well-cut trousers with forgiving waistbands paired with button down shirts. Afterward, I can resell these pieces and return them to the circular fashion economy. I wish more influencers explored secondhand shopping and creative ways to maintain personal style during pregnancy rather than presenting oversized clothing, exposed bellies, or maternity wear as the only options.

My later father-in-law, Dr. Robert L. Burman, earned his doctorate in 1962 working on a seminal series of electron-neutrino geometry experiments. As a nuclear and particle physicist at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) his research focused on the nature of neutrinos, particularly as understood through pions and other meson particles, and he designed and built the LANL low-energy pion channel. 

His loved ones — who emphatically are not scientists — used to joke that his career consisted of looking for things that didn’t exist. So we are tickled by Dr. Halzen’s assertion that “I never did anything close to reality in my career.”

Miss you, Bob. Physicists are indeed a special breed.

Either yoga, sports, stretching, dance, walking, swimming, biking, trampoline, skating; the list goes on, as options and we get to choose how to move. Carving out that time means dinner will be delayed, bedtime moves later but the reward of physical is worth the sacrifice. I bet you workers who are doing those kind of tasks for years suffer more problems than people typically reading the NYT like to think.  Concrete is all over too and will have a lot of silica in it too depending on the aggregate mix ... and no, they do not test everything on massive scale.

There is some genetic range and a difference between some exposure and getting pummeled daily. The claim is nonsense. I worked on Neural Networks a couple of years back (before they were a thing) and anyone claiming they understand what is happening, should win the next Field Medal or is an imposter. 

The problem itself is pretty straight forward: we don't have the maths to solve the problem. Even the most complex math we've ever been able to solve looks like elementry school task in comparison to the complexity of the functions that neural networks (the core component of LLMs) are approximating.

What we've manage to do is just fumble our way through to something that works and we understand the really basics of it, but it's like monkeys trying to operate a computer: we know certain buttons do something, but deviate from the recipe and we fall off a cliff. 

That's ok, that's how progress has always been made: we first figured out something that worked and then later figured out *why* something worked. But any researcher claiming they have solved it within the next 10 years is either a fraud or found a way to use AI to solve the underlying math problems.

comments.name: Jason Knox
comments.body:
The UK should resolve the reparations question definitively rather than leave it to fester. A principled route would be to invite Commonwealth governments to submit formal damage assessments, so that the debate rests on a quantified, scrutinised figure rather than competing moral claims and rhetoric.

Once the aggregate liability is known, the decision belongs to the people who would bear it. Reparations would be financed through taxation, falling on every UK taxpayer, so a binding referendum is the legitimate mechanism. It would also raise an unusual question of intergenerational justice: the public would be asked to compensate not the original victims but their descendants, several generations removed, using funds raised from citizens who include many with no ancestral link to the wrongs in question. Reasonable people differ on whether that obligation exists, which is precisely why it warrants democratic consent rather than executive decision.

If voters reject payment, the matter should be treated as settled. A clear mandate, reached transparently and with the full costs in view, would give both sides finality, and that is something the present, open-ended debate cannot offer.

Back in the early 1980s, I went to see the Grateful at one of their many runs at the Greek Theater on the Berkeley campus. My friends and I wanted to see all three shows that weekend, but we didn't want to camp, so we booked a cheap hotel room on University Avenue. I don't remember the name, but it was a two  story brick building that wrapped around a small parking lot.

After the first show, we came back to our room and we realized that the whole hotel was filled with Deadheads. The parking lot was filled with people playing tapes of the performance, milling around, enjoying each other's company (and a few refreshments) into the wee hours.

I remember seeing a couple, who seemed to be the hotel's proprietors. They looked like they might be immigrants from the far east. They were watching all of this in what appeared to be wide eyed wonder. The Dead and the traveling circus that followed them around were still a countercultural thing that was not well known in the mainstream back then, and they were clearly wondering: Who were all these crazy people? What was this strange music? Why was no one complaining about the noise?

This went on all weekend.

Just a shard of memory, a small remembrance of things past jarred loose by this article. Believe it if you need it.

Drama on a screen can be deeply moving if done well, or transport us to other worlds, contemporary or imaginary. It seems magical, but it’s really the end result of master professionals and artists combining their talents learned in years of work and development. Scott, like Rylance and McKellen and Metcalf, connect with their audiences in the moment, in real time, and the shock of emotional recognition is often transcendent. And they do it 6-8 times a week. The stock market has never been a good indicator of China’s economy. Even during the good years, China’s stock market performance was often mediocre, sometimes even worse. China is unlikely to produce a stock market that matches the US for many obvious reasons.

Today, China faces structurally weak confidence and significant economic headwinds, yet the government doesn’t seem overly concerned. So far, we have only seen small stimulus measures here and there. But in the long run, China will need to address these problems before it is too late.

Relying on exports alone is not a solution to sustainable economic growth. It creates vulnerabilities, even when China is exporting increasingly high-value-added goods. The only viable path to long-term economic health is to strengthen domestic consumption, particularly in the service sector.

Take India, for instance: its service sector accounts for roughly 60% of GDP, while China’s share hovers around 55%. In the US, it is around 80%. China will need to rebalance its economy toward domestic consumption and services if it wants to sustain growth over the long term.

Putting a limit on computers can stress students out as they try to chase this time limit and turn their work in. At my school, teachers teach at different paces and often, we are not allowed to work on the work until the teacher is done speaking, if there is a screen time limit, it makes it difficult to finish the work and it causes us to rush. If you use computers at school frequently, you'd have to stress if you saved enough time for the next class, and overall schools will become a very chaotic environment, student classwork grades will decline. A better fix for this issue of screenagers would be having software that can monitor what they are doing rather than limiting them a specific amount of time. comments.body: What a wonderful Idea for an exhibition and an informative article. Slowed down, ragtime pervaded much the second efflorescence of Tin Pan Alley. The syncopated melodies of ragtime allowed for more natural declamation of speech in later settings of lyrics (albeit with gentler and less pervasive syncopation), but stride bass (again, used very subtly) underlies many songs in some variety of duple meter.
